A third project valued at about $60,000 is expected to be awarded within 90 days, and management expects about $600,000 in revenue from the client over the next 12 months. ZenaTech, Inc. is a B2i Digital Featured Company. See the company's in-depth profile at: https://b2idigital.com/zenatech-1 School project work is under way, and once panels are installed, the opportunity shifts to recurring service: • Field data capture is complete at the first six school sites, now in processing • Management believes a drone can capture a full 10-acre campus in the same time a static scan takes for a 2-acre parking lot, or less. ZenaTech is running a proof of concept on three of the sites, two of them complete • Solar clients are already asking about infrared drone inspections and panel cleaning, work ZenaTech plans to offer with its IQ Square The contracts cover as-built surveys of school parking lots where solar canopies will be built over parking stalls. "Solar developers can’t design a single array until they have precise site data, and that first survey is where drones change the economics," said Shaun Passley, Ph.D., ZenaTech CEO. Read the full release: https://www.zenatech.com/zenatechs-drone-as-a-service-enters-solar-surveying-market-with-u-s-school-contract-wins-targeting-600000-in-revenue-from-first-solar-client/ ZenaTech, Inc. (Nasdaq: ZENA) (FSE: 49Q) (BMV: ZENA) is a technology company that specializes in AI autonomy drone platforms to transform commercial, government, and defense sectors. Its subsidiaries include drone manufacturing through ZenaDrone, a global Drone as a Service (DaaS) business, and an enterprise SaaS division of software brands. The Company is executing an acquisition-led DaaS roll-up strategy to digitize and automate legacy service industries including land surveys and inspections, driving drone-based scalable and recurring revenue growth. With an operating footprint spanning North America, Europe, the Middle East, Asia, and Australia, ZenaTech is advancing AI drones for agriculture and logistics, as well as ISR, cargo, and counter-UAS applications for U.S. defense and NATO allies. The company is investing in next-generation technologies, including drone swarms, quantum computing, and advanced AI autonomy to capture long-term opportunities in key markets through its R&D initiatives. items.title: Tesla announced its official entry into the Argentine market on November 20, opening a showroom on the first floor of Unicenter shopping mal
items.content_excerpt: Tesla announced its official entry into the Argentine market on November 20, opening a showroom on the first floor of Unicenter shopping mall, where customers will be able to explore its vehicles and test-drive a fleet of 10 cars. The company has not confirmed which models will be available, but the Model 3 and Model Y are the leading candidates, following their successful regional launches in Uruguay. Pricing remains uncertain, with two possible scenarios. A traditional importer cost structure could put the Model 3 at approximately $60,000 and the Model Y at $65,000. However, Tesla's direct-sales model, existing regional pricing and Argentina's new vehicle import regime could allow significantly lower prices of around $45,000 for the Model 3 and $50,000 for the Model Y. In Uruguay, the Model 3 starts at $32,990, offering up to 534 km of WLTP range, while the Model Y starts at $36,490 with up to 466 km of range. $TSLA

And not every correction means the market was irrational.

items.title: Microsoft is ending its AI computing capacity rental agreement with Oracle after declining to renew the contract and gradually disconnecting
items.content_excerpt: Microsoft is ending its AI computing capacity rental agreement with Oracle after declining to renew the contract and gradually disconnecting leased capacity in recent months, according to Bloomberg. The decision reflects a broader reassessment of multibillion-dollar cloud commitments as Microsoft evaluates its computing needs. The rented infrastructure reportedly became less useful because Oracle's servers relied on older-generation Nvidia chips that no longer met Microsoft's evolving AI workload requirements. The agreement, announced in 2023, helped Microsoft secure additional computing capacity for its AI-powered Bing search engine. Its total value was not disclosed. Microsoft declined to comment, while Oracle said demand for its AI infrastructure remains strong, including for older-generation GPUs. Oracle also said in September that it was renewing four-year-old GPU contracts at premiums of approximately 20% over original pricing. $MSFT $ORCL $NVDA

items.title: $EOSE 🤙 $AMZN’s Sunstone project in Oregon is permitted for up to 1.2 GW of solar and 7.2 GWh of battery storage. The $EOSE angle is easy to
items.content_excerpt: $EOSE 🤙 $AMZN’s Sunstone project in Oregon is permitted for up to 1.2 GW of solar and 7.2 GWh of battery storage. The $EOSE angle is easy to miss. Pine Gate, the original developer, included zinc alongside lithium-ion in its application and already had a separate 500 MWh agreement with Eos. Amazon hasn’t announced a battery supplier, and 7.2 GWh is the permit ceiling. But Eos already has a 100 MWh project with MN8 serving Google’s data centers. If Amazon chooses zinc at Sunstone, that would be another signal that non-lithium storage is finding a place in hyperscaler energy infrastructure.

items.title: $APLD My theory is that Wes’s NYC trip this week was about more than television. He appeared on CNBC’s Squawk on the Street on Monday, Novem
items.content_excerpt: $APLD My theory is that Wes’s NYC trip this week was about more than television. He appeared on CNBC’s Squawk on the Street on Monday, November 2, and Fox Business on Friday, November 6. I think Wes was in NYC to advance, and possibly finalize, financing for Polaris Forge 3, Delta Forge 1 and Delta Forge 2. There is a reason those three projects come to mind. On the October 7 earnings call, CFO Saidal Mohmand specifically identified those exact three campuses as the next projects requiring financing. He then said: “We are already in active discussions with leading lending institutions.” He also explained the intended structure: preferred equity from Macquarie, followed by project level debt. So I am not guessing whether a financing process exists. Management told us it was underway a month before this trip. These are substantial projects with signed customers, not speculative developments looking for tenants. Polaris Forge 3 and Delta Forge 1 each account for 300 MW, and Delta Forge 2 adds 210 MW. Together, that is 810 MW and approximately $20.2 billion in base-term contracted revenue. Management said all three are leased to the same tier-one investment-grade hyperscaler under 15-year take-or-pay agreements. We know that tenant is $META. The October filing described all three as under construction, with initial service at Delta Forge 1 targeted for the first half of 2027. There is a compelling reason to get the financing done now. Now look at where two of $APLD’s established financing partners operate. Goldman Sachs is at 200 West Street in Manhattan. Goldman led APLD’s $300 million bridge financing in May and arranged its corporate revolving credit facility. Macquarie’s Americas headquarters is at 660 Fifth Avenue. Its APLD framework contemplated up to $5 billion, including rights to invest another $4.1 billion across future projects. Those future investment rights are not the same as committed funding for these campuses, but Macquarie is the partner management explicitly named for the equity portion. These are existing business relationships, not banks I picked out of a directory. There are other established financing relationships in Manhattan, too. Morgan Stanley, with its headquarters at 1585 Broadway, represented the initial purchasers in $APLD’s $2.35 billion secured-bond offering in November 2025. SMBC, with offices at 277 Park Avenue, led the earlier $375 million Ellendale financing. Mizuho, RBC, Santander and Wells Fargo also participated as arrangers on APLD’s revolver. Wes would not need to start from scratch to put together a series of financing meetings in New York. That does not establish that any particular meeting occurred, but it makes the location relevant. I do not know whether Wes met these firms this week or whether any agreement reached the signing stage. I am not claiming inside information or promising an announcement on Monday. But when management identifies three campuses needing capital, confirms active lender discussions, and already works with major financing firms in Manhattan, I think financing is a reasonable explanation for at least part of the NYC trip. NYC is where the badly needed money for the needed financing is. My hypothesis is that Wez was there to move those deals toward closing, with the TV appearances providing an opportunity to tell the broader story. A financing announcement on acceptable terms would be the evidence that matters.

items.content_excerpt: Meta Platforms launched Spaces, a new feature in its Muse AI app that allows users to create personalized, interactive workspaces simply by describing what they want. Users can build custom tools such as gift trackers, daily word games, project dashboards, travel planners and shopping hubs, organizing them within the app's sidebar or main tabs. Spaces can connect to other applications and automatically update information in the background, including concert dates, price changes, savings progress, school events and calendar schedules. Users can also add notes, edit content and track items directly within each workspace. Other potential applications include podcast production, freelance client management, small-business order tracking and music discovery. The feature is available immediately across all platforms supporting Muse. Meta is also exploring collaborative sharing capabilities and introducing specialized AI models trained using insights from Muse Wonder. $META

items.content_excerpt: $GOOGL Problems: In a significant departure from Warren Buffett's famous reservations about technology stocks, the new CEO started cutting checks soon after he took on the job. In just a few months, he handed $10 billion to Google parent Alphabet Inc. to support its AI-related investments and plowed another $930 million into Bending Spoons SpA, an Italian conglomerate that uses the technology to transform businesses. But with cracks in the AI trade starting to show, Berkshire's sudden push may appear ill-timed. "I do think that part of this may be a conscious decision to increase their exposure," said Cathy Seifert, an analyst for CFRA Research. "One has to ask the question though, is it a little late?" Since June, Alphabet's Class A and Class C shares have tumbled more than 24% and are now trading below the discounted price at which Berkshire acquired them — prompting some to wonder whether its bet on the firm is a stinker.

items.title: $AVGO People keep repeating “circular financing” without understanding the actual structure. What Broadcom is doing with Anthropic is much c
items.content_excerpt: $AVGO People keep repeating “circular financing” without understanding the actual structure. What Broadcom is doing with Anthropic is much closer to equipment leasing, not traditional circular financing. Banks and institutional investors finance an SPV that purchases Broadcom’s AI hardware and leases it to Anthropic. Broadcom isn’t simply giving Anthropic money to buy its own chips. There is a legitimate risk, however: customer default and residual asset value. If Anthropic cannot meet its lease obligations AND the hardware has lost most or all of its value, Broadcom could face substantial losses under its residual-value guarantee. That’s the real concern. The same general customer-solvency question applies to OpenAI, although its contracts are different. Credit risk and asset depreciation are legitimate arguments. Calling every financing arrangement “circular financing” isn’t analysis.

items.title: $AVGO $NVDA $AMD $MSFT Every market correction brings the same argument: “AI is another dot-com bubble.” Really? Let’s compare the numbers.
items.content_excerpt: $AVGO $NVDA $AMD $MSFT Every market correction brings the same argument: “AI is another dot-com bubble.” Really? Let’s compare the numbers. March 2000 — Forward P/E: * CSCO: 130x * ORCL:120x * MSFT:60x * INTC:47x November 2026 — Trailing P/E / Forward P/E: * $AVGO: 37.4x / 16.9x * $NVDA: 23.6x / 15.4x * $MSFT: 27.7x / 25.6x * $AMD: 97.3x / 30.4x Even the S&P 500 trades at approximately 17.7x forward earnings today. The difference? Today’s AI leaders are generating enormous revenues, real profits and cash flow, with substantial earnings growth. Sure, some valuations are stretched, and forward estimates aren’t guaranteed. But comparing Broadcom at 17x forward earnings or Nvidia at 15x with Cisco at 130x during the dot-com bubble is simply ignoring the numbers. Not every technology boom is a bubble. And not every correction means the market was irrational.

items.content_excerpt: $AUPH **AUPH — Tidmarsh countersues Aurinia and Kevin Tang for defamation.** - Former FDA CDER director George Tidmarsh filed a 23-page complaint Oct 30 in Maryland federal court, alleging Aurinia and board chair Tang gave false bribery/abuse-of-authority accusations to senior FDA officials a year ago, triggering his removal. - This is the other side of a year-old dispute: Aurinia sued Tidmarsh Nov 2, 2025, the day he resigned as CDER director, over a LinkedIn post questioning Lupkynis's clinical benefit; Aurinia claimed its shares fell over 20% (~$350M erased). - The complaint also alleges former CBER director Vinay Prasad may have helped instigate the accusations after an internal dispute — but it does not establish that, and Prasad is not a defendant. - Damages unspecified beyond the $75K federal threshold; jury trial demanded.

$APLD My theory is that Wes’s NYC trip this week was about more than television. He appeared on CNBC’s Squawk on the Street on Monday, November 2, and Fox Business on Friday, November 6. I think Wes was in NYC to advance, and possibly finalize, financing for Polaris Forge 3, Delta Forge 1 and Delta Forge 2. There is a reason those three projects come to mind. On the October 7 earnings call, CFO Saidal Mohmand specifically identified those exact three campuses as the next projects requiring financing. He then said: “We are already in active discussions with leading lending institutions.” He also explained the intended structure: preferred equity from Macquarie, followed by project level debt. So I am not guessing whether a financing process exists. Management told us it was underway a month before this trip. These are substantial projects with signed customers, not speculative developments looking for tenants. Polaris Forge 3 and Delta Forge 1 each account for 300 MW, and Delta Forge 2 adds 210 MW. Together, that is 810 MW and approximately $20.2 billion in base-term contracted revenue. Management said all three are leased to the same tier-one investment-grade hyperscaler under 15-year take-or-pay agreements. We know that tenant is $META. The October filing described all three as under construction, with initial service at Delta Forge 1 targeted for the first half of 2027. There is a compelling reason to get the financing done now. Now look at where two of $APLD’s established financing partners operate. Goldman Sachs is at 200 West Street in Manhattan. Goldman led APLD’s $300 million bridge financing in May and arranged its corporate revolving credit facility. Macquarie’s Americas headquarters is at 660 Fifth Avenue. Its APLD framework contemplated up to $5 billion, including rights to invest another $4.1 billion across future projects. Those future investment rights are not the same as committed funding for these campuses, but Macquarie is the partner management explicitly named for the equity portion. These are existing business relationships, not banks I picked out of a directory. There are other established financing relationships in Manhattan, too. Morgan Stanley, with its headquarters at 1585 Broadway, represented the initial purchasers in $APLD’s $2.35 billion secured-bond offering in November 2025. SMBC, with offices at 277 Park Avenue, led the earlier $375 million Ellendale financing. Mizuho, RBC, Santander and Wells Fargo also participated as arrangers on APLD’s revolver. Wes would not need to start from scratch to put together a series of financing meetings in New York. That does not establish that any particular meeting occurred, but it makes the location relevant. I do not know whether Wes met these firms this week or whether any agreement reached the signing stage. I am not claiming inside information or promising an announcement on Monday. But when management identifies three campuses needing capital, confirms active lender discussions, and already works with major financing firms in Manhattan, I think financing is a reasonable explanation for at least part of the NYC trip. NYC is where the badly needed money for the needed financing is. My hypothesis is that Wez was there to move those deals toward closing, with the TV appearances providing an opportunity to tell the broader story. A financing announcement on acceptable terms would be the evidence that matters.

$AVGO People keep repeating “circular financing” without understanding the actual structure. What Broadcom is doing with Anthropic is much closer to equipment leasing, not traditional circular financing. Banks and institutional investors finance an SPV that purchases Broadcom’s AI hardware and leases it to Anthropic. Broadcom isn’t simply giving Anthropic money to buy its own chips. There is a legitimate risk, however: customer default and residual asset value. If Anthropic cannot meet its lease obligations AND the hardware has lost most or all of its value, Broadcom could face substantial losses under its residual-value guarantee. That’s the real concern. The same general customer-solvency question applies to OpenAI, although its contracts are different. Credit risk and asset depreciation are legitimate arguments. Calling every financing arrangement “circular financing” isn’t analysis.
